analysis.one_liner: Ends the bank bailout's asset purchases, replaces them with paid insurance, and cuts taxes on repatriated corporate profits.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees with no cosponsors on the day it was introduced, the bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have immediately shut down the Treasury's brand-new bailout authority, ending the government's power to buy troubled assets and bank stock, and instead required Treasury to run a program where banks paid premiums to insure their troubled mortgage-backed securities. It also would have let corporations bring foreign profits home while deducting 85% (or 100%, if invested in distressed debt) of the tax owed, so long as they filed a "domestic reinvestment plan" promising to spend the money on hiring, training, infrastructure, or research.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational corporations with large offshore profits would get the biggest direct benefit: an 85% tax deduction (100% for cash invested in distressed debt) on dividends from their foreign subsidiaries. Banks and other holders of troubled mortgage-backed securities would gain federal guarantees on those securities. Taxpayers would benefit only if swapping outright purchases for premium-funded insurance avoided the losses and favoritism risks of the government buying bank stock — though the guarantees still put taxpayers behind those securities.

how_it_helps.text: Immediately terminates Treasury's authority under the bailout law to purchase troubled assets, including preferred stock or other equity in financial institutions — ending the program of direct government injections into banks.

Requires Treasury, within 60 days, to establish a program insuring troubled residential and commercial mortgage-backed securities (those originated or issued on or before March 14, 2008), with the authority expiring December 31, 2009 unless Treasury certifies an extension to Congress with its expected cost to taxpayers.

Lets corporations deduct 85% of cash dividends received from their controlled foreign corporations (100% if the money is invested in distressed debt for at least a year), conditioned on a domestic reinvestment plan covering worker hiring and training, infrastructure, research and development, or capital investment.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the unoffset tax deduction, and taxpayers backstop the new guarantee program if premiums fail to cover losses on the insured securities. Banks would give up the capital injections but would have to pay premiums for the insurance in their place.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers backstopping guarantees; Treasury loses revenue

drawbacks.text: The insurance program is mandatory, not optional, and puts taxpayers directly behind troubled residential and commercial mortgage securities — the government guarantees losses on securities held by the same institutions that packaged them, so if premiums are set too low, taxpayers absorb the shortfall.

The repatriation tax break is policed by a 'domestic reinvestment plan' approved by the company's own president or CEO and its own board, and it counts 'the financial stabilization of the corporation' and one-year purchases of distressed debt as qualifying uses — conditions loose enough that companies could route the cash to balance-sheet repair rather than jobs.

The dividend deduction comes with no revenue offset, and terminating the purchase authority immediately — weeks after the bailout law passed, during a credit freeze — would have stripped Treasury of a tool it was already using to put capital into banks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The insurance-instead-of-purchases design had genuine taxpayer-protection logic: banks paying premiums for guarantees is a cleaner deal than the government guessing at asset prices, and the bill adds a hard sunset and a cost certification for extensions. But the bill undercuts its own populism with Section 4: an 85–100% deduction on repatriated foreign profits, with no revenue offset and a reinvestment requirement the company's own executives certify, that even lists corporate 'financial stabilization' as a qualifying use. As written, the tax title was a large, loosely policed gift to multinationals, and the guarantee title still left taxpayers holding the risk.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the closing weeks of the 110th Congress with no cosponsors, referred to two committees, and never heard from again before Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Louie Gohmert introduced the bill on November 20, 2008, about seven weeks after the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act created the bailout program it would amend.
The same day, the House referred it to the Financial Services Committee and, for the tax provisions, the Ways and Means Committee.
Not a single member of either party cosponsored the bill, no hearing or vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bailout program continued as written: Treasury kept injecting capital into banks in exchange for stock, and multinational corporations never got a discounted window to repatriate foreign profits. Because the bill had zero cosponsors and no committee ever touched it, its death changed little that was not already the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bailout program and the banks receiving funds

for.name: Louie Gohmert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 20, 2008; it attracted no cosponsors from either party

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral for its repatriation tax provisions and took no action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the fight never took a partisan shape on the record; the bill's only support was a single conservative Republican, and zero members of either party signed on as cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill revives a repatriation tax holiday: corporations could deduct 85–100% of dividends from their foreign subsidiaries, with the reinvestment plan certified by the company's own executives and 'financial stabilization of the corporation' counting as a qualifying use. It is an unoffset transfer from the Treasury to companies with large offshore profits, echoing the 2004 holiday whose cash flowed mainly to buybacks rather than jobs.

industries.industry: Banks and holders of mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: The bill takes away the equity-purchase program Treasury was using to inject capital into banks, but replaces it with mandatory Treasury insurance of their troubled mortgage-backed securities. The guarantee protects the holders of those securities while leaving taxpayers behind the risk if premiums prove inadequate.
